title: We Need to Involve Everyone: AI isn’t Just Another “EdTech” Tool
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard argues that treating AI as just another piece of educational technology, and leaving the discussion to ed-tech specialists, underestimates its impact on learning, relationships, security and ethics. He lists how AI differs from earlier tools: it can do teachers' and students' work, converse, inspire attachment and anger, rival or exceed human knowledge, tutor around the clock and simulate human traits. He concludes that the human side of teaching becomes the most important asset. He then names the groups who must be at the table, including ed-tech staff, communications experts, standards designers, ethicists, historians, psychologists, teachers, religious leaders and general thinkers. The text as supplied repeats its opening section, but the argument is clear.
points: The article's central claim is that you do not relate to a SmartBoard the way you relate to an AI, so the usual ed-tech framing fails.
AI can produce the work that earlier technologies only helped humans do, and can converse, tutor and simulate humanity.
Learning standards and assessments, such as writing expectations in a post-plagiarism world, will have to change.
Responding well requires many kinds of expertise beyond ed-tech, from ethics and psychology to history and teaching.
quotes: The simple reality is that you don’t relate to a SmartBoard the way you relate to an AI.
AIs can now produce most of that content and most of your students’ content.
Since AIs will understand the content as well or better than you, what you bring to the table as a human will be the most important thing.
But since their writing with a co-pilot should be substantially better than their writing without one, how should our writing standards change?
Many students will fear their efforts in school will not pay off with jobs in the future.
The integration of AI into society may be the biggest change in human history, and we need as many people as possible to think about how we relate to it.
